takeaways: Inflation cooled again — July CPI rose just 0.1%, bringing annual inflation to 3.4% and core to 2.5%, easing pressure for a September Fed rate hike and keeping the CRE refinancing window open.
GO Residential is buying H&R REIT's Sunbelt portfolio in a $2.8B deal adding 10,000+ multifamily units — the boldest move yet in the reset-basis consolidation wave sweeping multifamily.

Senior housing occupancy hit a record 89.9% in Q2 — the 20th straight quarterly gain — while inventory growth stayed under 1%, and Janus Living's $1B acquisition spree shows institutional capital piling in.

items.headline: July CPI cools to 3.4%, easing September rate-hike pressure
items.summary: Consumer prices rose just 0.1% in July, with annual inflation at 3.4% and core at 2.5% — both down 0.1 point from June. The in-line print keeps the Warsh Fed positioned to hold rates at the Sept. 15-16 FOMC meeting, preserving a friendlier backdrop for CRE refinancing and senior housing acquisition debt.

items.headline: GO Residential grabs H&R's Sunbelt portfolio in $2.8B deal
items.summary: Meyer Orbach and Josh Gotlib's TSX-listed GO Residential REIT is acquiring 27 properties from Canada's H&R REIT — including the 23-property Lantower Sunbelt multifamily package (10,000+ units) plus stakes in Miami's River Landing and LIC's Jackson Park — mostly paid in GO shares, with $550M CAD corporate and $1.1B property-level debt assumed. The deal takes GO to 13,300+ units and positions it for REIT index inclusion. (via The Promote)

items.headline: Senior housing occupancy hits record 89.9% as supply stays thin
items.summary: NIC MAP data shows Q2 2026 occupancy climbed 0.4 points to 89.9% — the 20th consecutive quarterly increase — with occupied units up nearly 3,700 to a record 639,650 and 15 of 31 primary markets at or above 90%. Inventory growth stayed below 1% for the fifth straight quarter, sustaining pricing power for operators like Lloyd Jones.

items.headline: Janus Living crosses $1B in senior housing acquisitions this year
items.summary: Janus Living completed roughly $1.0 billion of senior housing acquisitions through August 3 across six transactions with six different operating partners — 18 communities totaling 2,475 units. The buying spree underscores how aggressively institutional capital is re-entering the sector as occupancy sets records.

items.headline: 350 Park capstack takes shape: $3.3B loan, Citadel anchors 1.05M sf
items.summary: Vornado exercised its option for a 36% stake in 350 Park Ave, with Ken Griffin at 60% and the Rudins at 4%; Citadel will anchor the tower with 1.05M sf. Steve Roth says the team is lining up a $3.3B construction loan (53% LTC, ~$1,700/sf basis) and teasing a 25% club-deal stake sale — a bet on Manhattan office rents now firmly in the $200s/sf. (via The Promote)

items.headline: Nvidia's $500B financing pact reshapes the AI capital pipeline
items.summary: Nvidia's loose $500 billion arrangement with Wall Street titans will juice financing for weaker AI players while leaving the chipmaker partly on the hook if things go wrong. Separately, Bank of America plans to deploy $250 billion toward U.S. data centers, energy, and critical minerals — capital flows with direct implications for CRE land and power markets. (via WSJ 10-Point)

items.headline: Record occupancy, but cautious lenders keep construction stalled
items.summary: McKnight's reports senior living occupancy at record highs while conservative construction lending keeps new development stalled — assisted living construction costs are up in early 2026 while starts remain thin. For existing operators, the supply-demand imbalance extends the runway on rate growth.

items.headline: Ventas boosts 2026 senior living investment 50% to $4.5B+
items.summary: Ventas is raising its 2026 senior living investment target from $3 billion to over $4.5 billion as the sector shifts from defensive positioning to proactive growth. Big-REIT capital chasing senior housing validates valuations and deepens the buyer pool for operators considering dispositions.

items.headline: Tariff refunds turbocharge earnings: $9.6B across 40+ companies
items.summary: Over 40 S&P 500 companies have reported some $9.6 billion in tariff refunds in the past quarter, with at least $2.1 billion in cash already received — Apple nearly $2.2B, Nike $986M, FedEx ~$800M. The unexpected earnings tailwind is arriving far faster than analysts warned. (via WSJ 10-Point)

items.headline: Retail investors sit on record $3 trillion in money-market cash
items.summary: Individual investors are holding more than $3 trillion in retail money-market funds — near record highs — and advisers are struggling to move it into bonds or real assets even as yields fall. A massive pool of sidelined capital that could migrate toward income-producing real estate as rates ease. (via WSJ 10-Point)

items.headline: Developer Josh Schuster gets 4 years for Ponzi scheme
items.summary: Silverback Development's Josh Schuster was sentenced to four years in federal prison for defrauding investors who thought their funds were equity in Manhattan development projects. Judge Valerie Caproni rejected his addiction defense: 'The issue with fraudsters is that it's really hard to know whether you're being sincere.' A reminder on sponsor-level due diligence. (via The Promote)

items.headline: CRE debt costs at 6.57% vs. 6.34% cap rates — razor-thin spread
items.summary: Average CRE borrowing costs are hovering near 6.57% against average cap rates of 6.34%, an exceptionally tight (negative) spread that pressures levered buyers. Still, Colliers forecasts a 15-20% jump in 2026 sales activity as institutional and cross-border capital returns to the market.

items.headline: North Korean operatives used AI and stolen IDs to infiltrate U.S. jobs
items.summary: A year-long WSJ investigation found thousands of North Korean operatives using stolen identities and AI tools to land remote jobs at U.S. companies — one team infiltrated at least eight firms in months — funneling millions to Kim Jong Un's regime. A sharp warning for any company hiring remote workers, including back-office real estate roles. (via WSJ 10-Point)

items.headline: AI adoption in property management jumps to 58%, but automation lags
items.summary: AI adoption in property management leapt from 20% in 2024 to 58% in 2025, yet only 8% of companies have fully automated any process. The gap between experimentation and execution means operators who operationalize AI — leasing bots, billing, document intelligence — still have a first-mover edge.

items.headline: Hassabis pitched an AI oversight body before DeepMind exit
items.summary: Before stepping down as Google DeepMind CEO, Demis Hassabis pitched government officials and rival AI lab leaders on creating an independent safety entity to set guardrails for artificial general intelligence — a signal of where AI governance debates are heading. (via WSJ 10-Point)

items.headline: JPMorgan: 71% of business leaders confident despite tougher economy
items.summary: JPMorgan's 2026 Business Leaders Outlook finds 71% of leaders confident in their own company's performance. New products/services top the strategy list (58%, up from 53%), with strategic partnerships and investments rising to 49% — growth plays over cost-cutting.

items.headline: Intern-to-hire conversion jumps to 63.1% as AI takes menial work
items.summary: 63.1% of interns converted into full-time employees last year, up from 50.6% two years ago. With AI absorbing routine tasks, companies are handing interns real responsibility — from leading projects to business trips — making internship programs a sharper talent pipeline. (via WSJ 10-Point)

items.headline: How Canary Wharf brought down the Reichmann empire
items.summary: The Promote's trilogy on Olympia & York concludes with Canary Wharf — the megaproject where the Reichmanns' creative financing and cinematic self-belief, the very traits that built one of history's greatest real estate empires, turned against them. A cautionary leadership tale for every developer. (via The Promote)

items.headline: 'Datamaxxers' turn AI into hyperpersonalized health coaches
items.summary: Health obsessives are feeding every biomarker and workout into AI systems that act as personalized trainers and assistants — the leading edge of 2026's data-driven wellness trend, with obvious crossover potential for wellness programming in senior living. (via WSJ 10-Point)

items.headline: Europe's new EES passport system is the curse word of the summer
items.summary: The EU's new automated entry/exit system — facial recognition and fingerprints instead of passport stamps — is producing wildly inconsistent waits for U.S. travelers, from breezing through to hours-long lines on the same trip. Worth planning around for fall trips abroad. (via WSJ 10-Point)

items.headline: Greek island-hopping dreams meet the 'vomit comet'
items.summary: High-speed ferries through the Aegean have become Odyssean ordeals — bucket-list trips that require an actual bucket when seasickness hits. WSJ's guide to island-hopping without the misery. (via WSJ 10-Point)

items.headline: Wellness 2026: the backlash against over-optimization begins
items.summary: The Global Wellness Summit's 2026 trends flag a bold return of pleasure and joy over relentless self-optimization, alongside wellness tackling nervous-system exhaustion and disaster preparedness — with August marking National Wellness Month.
